translations: A torrential downpour struck on the afternoon of the fifth day, forcing them to take shelter among the gnarled roots of an ancient cypress tree. The tree’s branches and leaves spread out like giant umbrellas, raindrops dancing on the tips with a crisp, rhythmic sound, as if the sky were drumming against the earth. The heavy rain poured down like a river set ablaze, splashing against the stone-paved path and sending up sprays of water, as if showcasing nature’s fury. Aman opened a newly shaved narrow bamboo slip, his fingers gliding lightly over the damp surface, feeling as though he were touching a stone just soaked by rain. With solemn care, he wrote: “Water’s nature is best guided, not just blocked.” He looked up toward the distant ridge, where the outlines of mountain peaks were faintly visible through the mist, like giants wrapped in fog. The old herb-gatherer beside him peeked over, chuckled, and said, “Young man, you’re missing a stroke on the right side of that character for ‘guide.’” Aman squinted closely and realized he had indeed missed a dot—his pen tip had been knocked off course by a raindrop while he rushed to dodge the dripping eaves. He bit his lip and retraced the stroke, but the ink bled out, forming a small, stubborn cloud-like blot that seemed to dance on the slip. As dusk deepened, the sky turned a deep blue from the rain, the clouds looked as if they had been splashed with ink, and the light at the horizon was swallowed by the mist, leaving only the swaying shadows of the cypress in the rain. Yu the Great stood on the ridge, gazing into the distance: the muddy river was turning a corner, scouring the boulders at the valley mouth and rolling away in white foam. He untied his bundle, took out a clay jar, scooped half a ladle of clear water, and poured it into his palm. Slowly tilting his arm, he watched the water flow along the lines of his palm, splitting when it hit a bump and pausing in a dip, before finally gathering into a single stream and falling to the bottom of the cliff. Raindrops jumped on the water’s surface in his palm, like tiny dancers performing. “Look at how it walks,” he said. Aman was stunned, then grabbed his brush handle, pressed it against his chin, and nodded vigorously, his mouth twitching slightly. “Hmm... it knows how to walk better than I do.” He looked up, rain dripping from his hair as if washing away the day’s dust. The sound of the rain and the roar of the river blended into a passionate symphony, as if telling them: Yu the Great’s plan was slowly unfolding, and the flow of the water was being guided by his careful hand. Aman patted his own shoulder lightly and smiled. “Uncle Yu, your technique is steadier than my handwriting.” Yu the Great smiled, a mix of kindness and determination flashing in his eyes, as if telling him: though the path to taming the floods is long, it leads to a bright end. The rain fell harder, and the wind shook the cypress branches, as if applauding their efforts. Aman tucked his brush into his sleeve, looked into the distance, and silently noted in his heart: the water’s path must be cleared, the mountain’s path must be channeled, and only through persistence could the floods finally return to the sea, the fields and villages reappear, and the Nine Provinces find peace.

On the morning of the seventh day, the sound of axes was the first to wake the mountain hollow. Yu the Great swung his pickaxe into the cracks of the green oak rock, the shock splitting the skin at the base of his thumb. He spat out the saliva mixed with the earthy taste of soil, blew on his palm, gripped his tool tighter, and kept digging. Aman crouched on the slope, recording: “Third quarter of the Mao hour, began splitting the eastern ridge gap.” Before he finished speaking, loose gravel from behind him tumbled down. Instinctively, he leaned back, and the back of his head thudded against a tree knot with a dull “thunk.” The bamboo slip bounced twice, and a drop of ink landed on the left side of the character for “gap,” turning it into a little black mole. A shepherd boy picked up a flat, round pebble and handed it over. “Uncle, use this to hold down your paper!” Aman rubbed his head, took the stone, and placed it on the corner of the slip, muttering, “It’s steadier than I am.”

During the midday break, everyone gnawed on cold wheat cakes. Aman unfolded a new page, ground ink with water, and wrote carefully, stroke by stroke: “Chisel the mountain to guide the water; use curved force rather than direct confrontation.” As he wrote the right-side radical of the character for “curved,” a bead of sweat rolled down from his temple into his sleeve. His brush suddenly slipped, pulling the hook too long and crossing half the character—it looked as if someone had poked it with a stick. The man sitting next to him, chewing on cake crumbs, glanced over and said, “That character for ‘curved’ looks quite aggrieved.” Aman blew on the wet ink, kept a straight face, and said, “It’s just showing off its strength on purpose.”

Work ended in the evening, and the rain returned. Aman wrapped his straw raincoat tight and wrote quickly: “Rain pours in the You hour, yet the ditch is already a foot deep, and the water drains slowly along the channel.” He had just closed the bamboo slip when a gust of wind blew his conical hat off. He reached out to catch it, but the mud underfoot suddenly sucked his boot with a “squelch.” His body twisted into a pretzel shape. His right hand clung desperately to the bamboo slip, while his left hand grabbed a mossy rock to keep from falling flat on his back. Three young men digging the ditch couldn’t hold back their laughter. Embarrassed and annoyed, Aman simply sat cross-legged in the mud, threw his head back, and shouted, “Laugh all you want! Wait until I carve today’s incident onto the ancestral stele!”

At night, more than ten bonfires were lit. Amid the flickering flames, people took turns wielding chisels to pry stones and carrying wood and soil. Aman curled up by the fire to dry his bamboo slips, his fingers numb from the cold but his hand never stopping. Suddenly, he heard the rhythmic song of ramming earth nearby, rough in tone but strong and unified: “Hey-yo—if you can’t bend the mountain, ask it to shift its shoulder!” Listening to it, Aman quietly scraped away the four characters he had originally written, “Human strength is limited,” and added a new line in the blank space: “When there are many people, even the mountain will make way.”
